from a first model to a refusal

Stories

Each story states a small problem, writes it as a .sol model, runs the built binary and reads the answer. The numbers and the figures come from the run, not from the prose.

  • A bakery decides what to bake
  • A van with room for 15 kilos
  • A night rota nobody dreads
  • Two depots, three shops
  • When the answer is no
  • Trust, then check
  • When it stops early

A bakery decides what to bake

Marta runs a small bakery. Today she has 40 kg of flour, 8 kg of butter and 10 oven hours. A batch of loaves takes 2 kg of flour, half a kilo of butter and an hour of oven, and sells for 12; a tray of croissants takes a kilo of flour, a kilo and a half of butter and half an oven hour, and sells for 18. A fraction of a batch is fine.

// A bakery has 40 kg of flour, 8 kg of butter and 10 oven hours today.
// Per batch: a loaf needs 2 kg flour, 0.5 kg butter, 1 oven hour and sells for 12;
// a tray of croissants needs 1 kg flour, 1.5 kg butter, 0.5 oven hour and sells for 18.
// A batch can be fractional (half a tray is fine), so this is a linear program.
var loaf   : real 0..20;
var tray   : real 0..20;

maximize sales: 12*loaf + 18*tray;

subject to
    flour:  2*loaf + 1*tray   <= 40;
    butter: 0.5*loaf + 1.5*tray <= 8;
    oven:   1*loaf + 0.5*tray <= 10;
solve run < bakery.sol
$ solve run < bakery.sol
{"status":"optimal","objective":148.8,"x":{"loaf":8.8,"tray":2.4},"verified":true,"max_violation":0.0,"stats":{"iterations":2,"rows":3,"columns":2}}

She writes it down as a model, and asks. The answer is not the obvious one: neither all loaves nor all croissants, but 8.8 batches and 2.4 trays. The figure shows why: butter and oven time are used up, flour is not. More flour would not help; a little more butter would. That is the thing a solver tells you that a spreadsheet guess does not.

A van with room for 15 kilos

Tomás drives a courier van that carries 15 kg. He has six parcels. Each is taken whole or left at the depot; the weights are 12, 2, 1, 4, 7 and 5 kg, and each pays a fee.

// A courier van carries at most 15 kg. Six parcels, each taken whole or left behind:
// weight in kg, and the fee the courier earns for delivering it.
param n   = 6;
param w   = [12, 2, 1, 4, 7, 5];
param fee = [4, 2, 1, 10, 8, 6];
param cap = 15;

var take[0..n] : bool;

maximize income: sum i in 0..n: fee[i] * take[i];

subject to
    weight: sum i in 0..n: w[i] * take[i] <= cap;
solve run < van.sol
$ solve run < van.sol
{"status":"optimal","objective":21.0,"bound":21.0,"x":{"take[0]":0.0,"take[1]":1.0,"take[2]":1.0,"take[3]":1.0,"take[4]":1.0,"take[5]":0.0},"verified":true,"max_violation":0.0,"stats":{"iterations":6,"rows":1,"columns":6,"nodes":7,"branched":4,"method":"dense"}}

Now the variables are yes-or-no, so solve branches: it solves the LP with fractions, finds a fractional parcel, and splits on it until the answer is whole. The heavy 12 kg parcel does not make the cut, for its fee; four parcels do, filling 14 of the 15 kg. stats.nodes says how many LPs it took.

A night rota nobody dreads

The ward needs one nurse on each of four night shifts and each nurse works one. Every nurse has scored every shift from 0 (happy) to 9 (would rather not). The head nurse wants the lowest total.

// Four nurses, four night shifts, one nurse per shift and one shift per nurse.
// dislike[i*n+j] is how much nurse i dislikes shift j (0 = happy, 9 = would rather not).
param n = 4;
param dislike = [3, 7, 2, 9,
                 6, 1, 8, 4,
                 5, 5, 3, 2,
                 9, 4, 6, 1];

var give[0..n, 0..n] : bool;

minimize unhappiness: sum i in 0..n: sum j in 0..n: dislike[i*n+j] * give[i,j];

subject to
    forall i in 0..n: one_shift_each: sum j in 0..n: give[i,j] == 1;
    forall j in 0..n: one_nurse_each: sum i in 0..n: give[i,j] == 1;
solve run < rota.sol
$ solve run < rota.sol
{"status":"optimal","objective":8.0,"bound":8.0,"x":{"give[0,0]":1.0,"give[0,"give[0,"give[0,"give[1,"give[1,1]":1.0,"give[1,"give[1,"give[2,"give[2,"give[2,2]":1.0,"give[2,"give[3,"give[3,"give[3,"give[3,3]":1.0,…},"verified":true,"max_violation":0.0,"stats":{"iterations":6,"rows":8,"columns":16,"nodes":1,"branched":0,"method":"dense"}}

This is an assignment problem, a model of rows that must equal one. The answer is the diagonal here, total 8; the search needed a single node because the LP relaxation was already whole. Assignment models are special: the LP relaxation of one always has a whole optimal vertex, so there was nothing to branch on.

Two depots, three shops

A wholesaler has two depots, holding 60 and 50 crates, and three shops that need 30, 40 and 25. Crates can be split between shops. A crate costs a different amount on each route.

// Two depots supply three shops. cost[i*3+j] is the price per crate from depot i to shop j.
// Depot 0 holds 60 crates, depot 1 holds 50. The shops need 30, 40 and 25. Crates can be split.
param cost = [4, 6, 9,
              5, 3, 7];
param stock = [60, 50];
param need  = [30, 40, 25];

var ship[0..2, 0..3] : real 0..100;

minimize freight: sum i in 0..2: sum j in 0..3: cost[i*3+j] * ship[i,j];

subject to
    forall i in 0..2: stock_limit: sum j in 0..3: ship[i,j] <= stock[i];
    forall j in 0..3: shop_need:   sum i in 0..2: ship[i,j] >= need[j];
solve run < depots.sol
$ solve run < depots.sol
{"status":"optimal","objective":445.0,"x":{"ship[0,0]":30.0,"ship[0,"ship[0,2]":15.0,"ship[1,"ship[1,1]":40.0,"ship[1,2]":10.0,…},"verified":true,"max_violation":0.0,"stats":{"iterations":4,"rows":5,"columns":6}}

A transportation LP, with real variables: nothing to branch on. The cheapest plan sends depot 0 to shop 0 and shop 2, and depot 1 to shop 1 and shop 2. The figure draws the flows to scale.

When the answer is no

Two kinds of no, and the tool keeps them apart. A model that cannot be read is refused with a repair; a model that reads fine but has no solution is an answer.

// A variable with no bounds: the checker refuses it before any solver sees it.
var x : real;
maximize x;
subject to c: x <= 4;
solve check
$ solve check < unbounded.sol
{"error":"solve.unbounded-domain","message":"a variable has no bounds","repair":"write the bounds: var x : real 0..10;","at":{"line":2,"col":5}}
# exit status 2
// Two parcels that cannot both be taken and must both be taken.
var a : bool;
var b : bool;
maximize a + b;
subject to
    both:   a + b >= 2;
    either: a + b <= 1;
solve run
$ solve run < cannot.sol
{"status":"infeasible","stats":{"iterations":1,"rows":2,"columns":2,"nodes":1,"branched":0,"method":"dense"}}

The first is a mistake in the model: a variable with no bounds is refused before any solver sees it, with the line to write. The second is not a mistake of the tool or the writer: two parcels that must both go and cannot both go. run says infeasible and exits 0, because that is a correct result.

Trust, then check

An answer can come from solve run, from HiGHS, from a colleague or from a model that guessed. solve verify does not care which.

solve verify
$ (cat van.sol; echo ---; solve run < van.sol) | solve verify
{"status":"verified","objective":21.0,"objective_checked":true,"tolerance":0.000001,"max_bound_violation":0.0,"max_integrality_violation":0.0,"max_row_violation":0.0,"variables":6,"rows":1,"proves":"feasibility and the objective value, not optimality"}
# someone hand-edits the answer to take the 12 kg parcel as well
$ (cat van.sol; echo ---; <take[0] changed to 1>) | solve verify
{"error":"solve.row-violated","message":"a constraint does not hold at the claimed values","repair":"the solution is infeasible; solve again","count":2,"violations":[{"rule":"solve.row-violated","what":"weight","value":11.0,"limit":0.000027},{"rule":"solve.objective-mismatch","what":"objective","value":4.0,"limit":0.000026}]}
# exit status 2

It reads the model and the claimed solution and re-evaluates both: bounds, whole numbers where the model says whole, every row, and the objective. Here the overloaded van is caught by the row weight, and the objective that no longer matches is caught with it. What it does not say is that an accepted answer is the best one: for that the gates hold the solver to HiGHS and, on integer models, to CP-SAT and SCIP.

When it stops early

A bigger model can take longer than you will wait. A limit makes the stop an answer.

solve run --node-limit 3
$ solve run --node-limit 3 < van.sol
{"status":"unknown","limit":"nodes","bound":22.857142857142858,"stats":{"iterations":3,"rows":1,"columns":6,"nodes":3,"branched":3,"method":"dense"}}
# exit status 1

With three nodes the search has found no whole answer yet, so the status is unknown; but it knows the optimum cannot exceed the bound. With an incumbent the status would be feasible and a gap would say how far the best known answer could be from the best possible. Either way the exit status is 1: not an error, not a finished proof.
